requirement:
Plain text defines no attachments. The file root and each `line` item have
empty attachment lists, including lines that begin with comment delimiters
from another language.
rationale:
**Obligation.** `requirements.sdk.sources.plain-text.attachments` has one obligation. The file root and every `line` item must have an empty attachment list. This includes lines that begin with comment delimiters from another language. The text has no other MUST, SHOULD or alternative clause.

**Test.** `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/outline_content.rs#fn[bundled_languages_classify_only_their_attachment_syntax]` carries a `{test}` reference to the subject. Its `test.txt` case parses `"# just text\n"` through `OutlineContent::from_source`. That input is a line starting with `#`, which is a comment delimiter in other languages such as Python, YAML and TOML. The test gathers `attachments` from every item with `snapshot.outline().items.iter().flat_map(|i| &i.attachments)`. It asserts that the collected list equals `vec![]`.

**Why this covers the obligation.**
- The collection spans every outline item, including the root and any `line` items. A non-empty attachment list on any of them would fail the assertion.
- The input is the named boundary case: a foreign-language comment delimiter at the start of a line.
- In the same loop, the other cases (`test.py`, `test.yaml`, `test.toml` and the rest) assert the non-empty attachment results for their languages. The `# just text` case therefore contrasts with the languages that do classify `#` lines as comments.

**Why no further scenarios are needed.** I read the implementation `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/mod.rs#fn[plain_text]` only to see whether it branches on delimiter text. It does not. It builds one `line` node per non-blank line and returns `comments: Vec::new()` and `annotations: Vec::new()` unconditionally. Delimiter-specific inputs such as `//`, `/*` or `<!--` therefore add no distinct input class.

I found no gaps, and the acknowledgments list is empty.
